_doc: T-0826. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 2 (Chicago and New York: Munsell, 1895) — THE HALF OF THE WORK T-0581 COULD NOT READ. That ticket read volume 1 and recorded, for each of the forty-nine lead surnames the Newberry index (T-0570) flagged against the WORK, what volume 1 says about it; but the Newberry cards do not say which volume they cite, so every ABSENT verdict it recorded was an absence from one book of two. This file and data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v2_lead_surnames.json close that: the same forty-nine surnames are searched across all 107,905 lines of volume 2 by the same instrument (tools/search_book_lead_surnames.py, whose --self-test re-derives every one of volume 1's 196 mechanical fields before it will run), and twenty passages earned a claim. WHAT VOLUME 2 IS: biographical memoirs and trade-by-trade chapters, compiled 1895, overwhelmingly about men who reached Chicago after 1850 — which is why 31 of the 49 surnames appear only outside the pre-1836 window. Its value to a town of July 1835 is concentrated in four things volume 1 does not give: two dated PRESENCE LISTS (the Baptist fourteen of 19 October 1833 and the Episcopal eleven of 1834), a brick yard and a tannery placed by street and by bank, a residence of Richard J. Hamilton with a block, and a second address for the Chicago Democrat's office. EVERY CLAIM IS transcription_mediated: this is the Internet Archive's machine OCR of the same UIUC copy volume 1 came from, no page image was read, and the quotes are committed WITH the OCR's faults because the gate rebuilds them character for character. The smoothed reading of each is in `normalized`. NO RECORD UNDER data/structures/, data/residents/, data/households/ OR data/businesses/ WAS EDITED BY THIS READING — the third acceptance clause of T-0581 binds T-0826 too: anything this volume dates and places before 1835-07-01 is offered to those layers under the ratified ladder IN THAT LAYER'S OWN PR.
generated_by: hand — T-0826. The `quote` of every claim was filled programmatically from the committed text at its own locator so that no transcription step stands between the file and the gate; everything else in each claim is authored. The printed page of every locator comes from tools/derive_book_folios.py, which re-derives the folio rule for THIS volume rather than assuming volume 1's.

claims.normalized: About the end of the Chicago Democrat's first year of publication its office was removed to a room over the hardware store of Jones & King, a few doors from its first location. A few weeks later it was compelled to suspend publication for want of paper, and the suspension ran from January 1, 1835 to May 20 following, with the exception of two issues on January 21 and March 25.
claims.describes_date: the removal is "about the end of its first year of publication" — the Democrat began 26 November 1833, so late 1834; the suspension is dated 1 January to 20 May 1835, which is BEFORE the scene date of 1835-07-01
claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME IS `jones`. A SECOND ADDRESS FOR THE DEMOCRAT'S OFFICE, stated as a relation to a business the project can place: a room over Jones & King's hardware store, "a few doors from its first location". T-0403 is open on exactly this question — whether the Democrat kept its 1834 corner through the scene date — and this sentence says it did not, without naming the street. The firm is dated independently at bk_mose2_002: William Jones and Byron King formed the hardware partnership in 1834, so the room is over a shop that existed when the paper moved into it. The compiler gives no street and no number, and nothing here may be turned into a coordinate; what it fixes is a RELATION.

claims.normalized: The first foundry in Chicago was erected in 1835. In 1834 William Jones and Byron King formed a partnership to deal in hardware; in 1835 W. B. Clarke became a partner and the firm name was changed to Jones, King & Co. The firm employed William Stow & Co. to erect a foundry, built on Polk street west of the south branch, and David Bradley of Syracuse came to Chicago as Stow's employee to assist in its construction. The first castings were made in December 1835.
claims.describes_date: 1834 for the hardware partnership — BEFORE the scene date of 1835-07-01; 1835 for Clarke's admission and the foundry, with the first castings December 1835, which is AFTER it
claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME IS `jones`. TWO DATES AND THE SCENE DATE FALLS BETWEEN THEM, which is the whole value of the passage. The hardware partnership of Jones and King is 1834 and belongs in the town of July 1835; the foundry on Polk street west of the south branch does NOT — its first castings are December 1835, five months late, and it goes to data/exclusions.json rather than to the scene. W. B. Clarke's admission is "1835" with no month and cannot be placed either side of the scene date.

claims.normalized: Mr. Granville T. Sproat arrived from Boston and established an English and classical school for boys, occupying for that purpose the First Baptist church, a small frame building located on South Water street near Franklin. Miss Sarah L. Warren, afterwards Mrs. Abel E. Carpenter, became an assistant in Mr. Sproat's school in the spring of 1834.
claims.describes_date: the spring of 1834 for Miss Warren joining the school; Sproat's arrival and the school's establishment are earlier and undated here — both BEFORE the scene date of 1835-07-01
claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME IS `carpenter`, and it is a MARRIED NAME acquired later — "afterwards Mrs. Abel E. Carpenter" — so it reaches no Chicago man of 1835 and the row's verdict says so. THE PASSAGE IS THE FIND, not the surname: the First Baptist church is given as a small frame building ON SOUTH WATER STREET NEAR FRANKLIN, which is a street and a cross street, the form data/structures/ can use. It is also a DOUBLE USE of one building — a Baptist meeting house on Sunday and a boys' school on weekdays — and the same building is where Rev. Isaac W. Hallam held the first Episcopal services on 19 October 1834 (bk_mose2_009). Nothing here dates the building itself.

claims.normalized: No term of court was held until 1834, and the first term was held not in the brick house in the fort — it is also denied that there was any brick house there — but in an unfinished loft in the "Mansion House", directly north of the present Tremont House; and the first case in that first term bore the name of John Dean Caton as attorney.
claims.describes_date: 1834 for the first term of court, and bk_mose2_005 of the same chapter dates the trial to the spring of 1834 — BEFORE the scene date of 1835-07-01
claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME IS `caton`. A USE AND A BEARING FOR A BUILDING THE PROJECT HOLDS: Cook county's first term of court sat in an unfinished loft of the Mansion House, and the Mansion House is placed by this sentence DIRECTLY NORTH OF THE TREMONT HOUSE. The Tremont of 1835 is not the Tremont of 1895 and the compiler writes "the present Tremont House", so the bearing is to the 1895 building and must not be resolved against the 1835 one without a second source; T-0385 is open on the 1835 Tremont's own position in Dearborn Street and this sentence does not settle it. The denial of the brick house in the fort is the compiler arguing with Governor Bross and is recorded as the disagreement it is, not adopted.

claims.normalized: Richard J. Hamilton lived first in the fort and, when that grew too crowded with the refugees, he moved to the Agency House; and in 1833, with Col. Owen, hired John Watkins to teach the little school in the old stable near by. At about this time he built his house on what is now Michigan street between Cass and Rush, where he lived for nineteen years.
claims.describes_date: 1833 for the school in the old stable, and "at about this time" for the house — so 1833 or thereabouts, BEFORE the scene date of 1835-07-01, but a date the compiler himself hedges
claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME IS `hall` (the passage above this one lists "the families of Davis, Hall and Pettigrew" at the Indian Creek killings of 1832, which is not Chicago and is not this claim). TWO THINGS THE PROJECT IS THIN IN, both here. A RESIDENCE WITH A BLOCK: Hamilton built his own house on what the compiler calls Michigan street between Cass and Rush, and lived in it nineteen years, which puts it in the town at the scene date. A SCHOOL IN A BUILDING ALREADY STANDING: the little school Watkins was hired to teach in 1833 sat in "the old stable near by" the Agency House, which is a use of an outbuilding and not a new structure. THE STREET NAMES ARE 1895 NAMES — the compiler says "what is now" — so the block must be resolved through the street-name history before any coordinate is derived, and the date is the compiler's own "at about this time" and not a stated year.

claims.normalized: The first drug store established in the place was by Philo Carpenter in the latter part of 1832. The next drug store was established in the spring of 1833 by Dr. Edmund Stoughton.
claims.describes_date: the latter part of 1832 for Carpenter's and the spring of 1833 for Stoughton's — both BEFORE the scene date of 1835-07-01
claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME IS `carpenter`. THE SECOND HALF IS NEW TO THIS PROJECT: volume 1 gives Carpenter as the town's first druggist and says nothing about a second drug store, and this names one — Dr. Edmund Stoughton's, spring 1833. A business with a proprietor, a trade and a year, and NO position at all: the sentence gives no street, no corner and no landmark, so it can reach data/businesses/ but not the scene. The surname is printed "Stoughtou" by the OCR and the smoothed reading is in `normalized`.

claims.normalized: The first Sunday school in Chicago was organized on August 19, 1832 by Luther Childs, assisted by Mrs. Seth Johnson, Mrs. Charles Taylor, the Misses Noble and Philo Carpenter. Its first sessions were held in a small frame building erected by Mark Beaubien near Mr. Noble's house; when the school was first opened the house in which it was held had neither doors nor windows and was very imperfectly roofed. Later it assembled at the house of Rufus Brown, within the stockade of the fort.
claims.describes_date: 19 August 1832 for the school's organization, and the two buildings in that order afterwards — all BEFORE the scene date of 1835-07-01, with no date for the move
claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME IS `carpenter`. A BUILDING WITH A BUILDER, A NEIGHBOUR AND A CONDITION: a small frame building erected by Mark Beaubien near Mr. Noble's house, which in August 1832 had NEITHER DOORS NOR WINDOWS and was very imperfectly roofed. The project holds Mark Beaubien and it holds the Noble house, so the relation is placeable, and the condition is the kind of material fact the renderer can carry — but it is a condition of 1832 and says nothing about 1835, by which time the building may have been finished, moved or gone. Rufus Brown's house inside the stockade is a second structure the same sentence places.

claims.normalized: Episcopal services were later held in a building afterwards known as Tippecanoe Hall, situated at the southeast corner of Kinzie and State streets, which was fitted up for the purpose at the expense of John H. Kinzie. Subsequently Mr. Kinzie donated two lots as a site for a permanent church building, at the intersection of Cass and Illinois streets.
claims.describes_date: UNDATED. The paragraph before it is dated 19 October 1834 and the word is "Later", so the fitting-up is after that and before the brick church the same passage goes on to describe; whether it is before or after 1835-07-01 this sentence does not say
claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME IS `hall`, and it is the BUILDING'S NAME and not a person — the row's verdict says so. A CORNER, WHICH IS THE FORM THE PROJECT WANTS, and a date the compiler does not give: the southeast corner of Kinzie and State streets, fitted up at John H. Kinzie's expense. THE DATE IS THE WHOLE QUESTION and it is open, so this claim may NOT be carried into the 1835 scene on its own; it is offered as a candidate that a second source must date. "Afterwards known as Tippecanoe Hall" is a name the building got later — the Tippecanoe campaign is 1840 — so the name is anachronistic for 1835 even if the building is not.

locator.original: Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 2, printed page 294 — and this one is READ BY HAND rather than by the derivation, off the head at line 34254, whose running head the OCR set as "niSTOET OF CHICAGO." and which tools/derive_book_folios.py still does not match. T-1024 rebuilt that derivation and this page is the one claim it did not reach: it reports the page carried between read folios 291 at line 33936 and 295 at line 34375, and the bare "294" at line 34253 above a head the pattern cannot see is what a human reads instead. claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME IS `hall`, AND THIS VOLUME CONTRADICTS THE OTHER ONE. Volume 1 gives Benjamin Hall, on Blanchard's authority through a block quotation, as "proprietor of the first tannery ever established there", arriving 1830 (bk_mose1_019). The project holds Miller's tavern, so the relation is placeable.

claims.normalized: Dr. John T. Temple put in operation in 1834 a stage line from Chicago to Peoria which, according to its own advertisement, left Chicago at 4 a.m., reached "Juliet" at 2 p.m. and Ottawa the first day, completing the trip to Peoria in two days. Caton, between whom and Dr. Temple there grew up an intimacy, as the young lawyer obtained a desk in the office and a sleeping room in the attic of the Temple building, which Dr. Temple had put up in 1833.

claims.normalized: The chosen elders of the first Presbyterian organization were Philo Carpenter, John Wright and Major Wilcox. claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME IS `black` and it is the BLACK HAWK WAR two paragraphs on, not a person — the same verdict volume 1 recorded for this surname. THE PASSAGE IS A CIVIC FACT WITH A FIGURE: section 16, the school section, sold in October 1833 for $38,895 on the petition of three-fourths of the township's legal voters. It bears on the land layer rather than the structures layer — the lots the town was built on in 1834-5 were sold at this auction — and the project holds no figure for it. The sum is a compiler's of 1895 and is quoted, not adopted.

locator.original: Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 2, printed page 157, read off the recto head at line 19005. The folio is READ off the running head and not counted, and the rule was re-derived for THIS volume rather than carried over from volume 1 (tools/derive_book_folios.py --audit): the page number stands alone on a line at the head of every verso, above "HISTORY OF CHICAGO.", and after the chapter title at the head of every recto; verso heads are even and recto heads are odd, and a numeral of the wrong parity for its side is refused and corrected inside its run where the run says which page it must be. T-1024 REBUILT THAT DERIVATION AND THIS LOCATOR IS ITS OUTPUT. Two faults had left the recto side unread: the verso head was searched for INSIDE a line rather than matched on the whole of one, so a sentence writing the phrase in prose (line 9941) was taken for a head and stole the recto numeral above it; and the recto head, which the rule always named, was never a head in its own right — it was consulted only to break a tie once the verso folio was already known. The volume prints 336 recto folios, 320 of them odd. Read as heads they carry the folio on 512 of 615 heads where the verso side alone carried 271 of 319.

claims.normalized: James H. Collins came to Illinois in 1833 and settled on a pre-emption claim at Holderman's grove, some sixty or seventy miles southwest of Chicago. In 1834 his former student Caton found him in great distress and arranged that, as soon as he should recover the use of his feet, then badly frozen, he should come to Chicago and join Caton in the practice of law. The partnership lasted but about a year, and Collins then formed another with Justin Butterfield.
claims.describes_date: 1834 for the arrangement; Collins's arrival in Chicago is "as soon as he should recover" and is NOT dated, so whether he was in the town on 1835-07-01 this passage does not settle
claims.notes: THE LEAD SURNAME IS `caton`. A LAW PARTNERSHIP — Caton & Collins — that the project does not hold, and an arrival the compiler leaves open: Collins agreed in 1834 to come to Chicago when his frozen feet mended, and the sentence never says when he came. So this is a CANDIDATE for the town of July 1835 and not a resident of it, and the honest reading is that the partnership existed at some point between 1834 and about 1836. Recorded so that a later run with a dated source can close it rather than re-read the volume.

claims.normalized: The Chicago Lyceum's library, kept in a room over P. F. W. Peck's store, held about twenty volumes. Two visitors to the settlement from New York, Charles Butler and Arthur Bronson, were moved by the sight of it and on their return home sent a donation of two hundred volumes.
claims.describes_date: The Lyceum's early years, which the chapter sets in the first half of the 1830s; the visit itself is NOT dated by this passage. What it does fix is the pair's relation to the town — visitors from New York who went home — and not a day.
claims.notes: READ FOR T-1017, which asked whether buying at the town's own school-section sale of October 1833 is itself a check that a name belonged to the town. ARTHUR BRONSON IS THE FOURTH LARGEST HAND AT THAT AUCTION — thirteen blocks under BRONSON and eight more under the register's spelling BROSON — and this is the town's own historians calling him a VISITOR FROM NEW YORK who went home again. That is what the ticket turned on: a sale whose biggest buyers travelled from New York to attend it cannot certify residence, so the purchase is corroboration and never an arm of the ruling rule (the arithmetic at data/research/land_sales/school_section_sale_1833.json, the ruling at resident_rulings.json -> questions_ruled -> T-1017, reasoned out at docs/RESEARCH/school_section_sale_1833.md). WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY, and the ruling does not make it say: it does not date the visit, it does not say Bronson was never at Chicago on 1 July 1835, and it does not identify this Arthur Bronson with the register's purchaser by anything but the name — that identification rests where it already rested, on the register's own BRONSON FREDERIC(K) beside him and on the old-settler death notices. It is evidence about the SALE, not about a card.
